clue.text: Chekhov offering expected to take off?

definitions.meaning: a play by Anton Chekhov, first staged in 1896
a shore bird that can be relied on to lift off into flight

explanation.surface: A Chekhov production is tipped to become a hit.
explanation.definitionFit: Chekhov wrote a play of that title, and the coastal bird it names is a creature that flies off.

clue.text: River setting for The Trial?

definitions.meaning: a chalk-stream in Hampshire, England, famous for trout fishing
a trial is an examination, which is something set

explanation.surface: Asks which river Kafka's novel The Trial was set beside.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital T on 'The Trial' points to Kafka's novel, but the clue only wants a trial in the sense of an exam that someone sets.
explanation.definitionFit: The English river shares its name with an exam, which is a trial you set for someone.

clue.text: Heroic story must be in the picture

indicators.note: in signals that the letters sit inside the run of words the picture

explanation.surface: A grand heroic tale really ought to be filmed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'be in' reads as part of the phrase 'be in the picture', meaning informed; here 'in' points to letters lurking inside 'the picture'.
explanation.definitionFit: An epic is a long narrative poem about heroes and their deeds.

clue.text: Belloc's book of Algerian impressions may it last for ever!

definitions.meaning: Hilaire Belloc's 1906 travel book about North Africa
a Latin motto wishing permanence, said of Venice by the theologian Paolo Sarpi

explanation.surface: A Belloc travel book on Algeria, with the wish that it endure.
explanation.definitionFit: Belloc took his title from the Latin blessing meaning 'let it be perpetual'.

clue.text: Tell-tale German tale-teller

definitions.meaning: British slang for an informer who betrays others to the police
Günter ..., German novelist of The Tin Drum

explanation.surface: A German storyteller who is also a sneak.
explanation.walkthrough: In British slang a 'grass' is someone who informs on others to the police.
explanation.definitionFit: Günter Grass was a German novelist, and the same word is slang for an informer.

clue.text: Some capital poems from Gavin Ewart

definitions.text: Some capital poems from Gavin Ewart

parts.words: Some capital poems from Gavin Ewart
parts.note: the title of Ewart's 1964 collection, which also names people of a capital city

explanation.surface: Praises certain excellent verses by the poet Gavin Ewart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'capital' looks like praise for the poems ('excellent') but refers to the British capital: Ewart's collection is named for its inhabitants.
explanation.definitionFit: Ewart's 1964 collection is titled after the residents of England's chief city.

clue.text: Graduate with church composer

parts.note: BA is a Bachelor of Arts, a graduate

explanation.surface: A graduate goes along with a composer of church music.
explanation.walkthrough: 'church composer' reads as one phrase, but 'church' gives letters and only 'composer' defines.
explanation.definitionFit: Johann Sebastian Bach was the German Baroque composer.

clue.text: Euripides heroine had romance shattered

indicators.note: shattered means broken into pieces, so the letters of had romance are rearranged

explanation.surface: A tragic heroine whose love affair was ruined.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shattered' rearranges HAD ROMANCE.
explanation.definitionFit: Hector's widow is the title figure of a tragedy by Euripides.

clue.text: Falstaff's prince, extremely funny betimes, twice annually

parts.note: Prince Hal, Falstaff's drinking companion in Shakespeare's Henry IV plays

indicators.note: extremely takes the extreme ends, the first and last letters, of funny

parts.note: betimes is an old word for early

explanation.surface: Shakespeare's prince is comic now and then, twice a year.
explanation.walkthrough: 'extremely' takes F and Y, the first and last letters of 'funny'.
explanation.definitionFit: Something done every six months happens two times in each year.

clue.text: French music critic assents in a new composition

indicators.note: a new composition puts the letters of assents in a into a fresh arrangement

explanation.surface: A French reviewer of music approves a newly written piece.
explanation.walkthrough: 'new composition' rearranges ASSENTS IN A. Camille Saint-Saëns wrote music criticism as well as composing.
explanation.definitionFit: Camille Saint-Saëns, best known as a composer, also wrote criticism on music.

clue.text: Strange Lido apparition, as he seemed to von Aschenbach

definitions.text: apparition, as he seemed to von Aschenbach

indicators.note: strange means odd or altered, so the letters of Lido are rearranged

explanation.surface: In Death in Venice, the boy on the Lido strikes von Aschenbach as a vision.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strange' rearranges LIDO. In Thomas Mann's Death in Venice, Aschenbach worships the boy Tadzio, seen on the Lido beach.
explanation.definitionFit: Aschenbach treats Tadzio as an object of worship, a vision of perfect beauty.

clue.text: Cowardly reference to satanic types?

definitions.meaning: a play by Noël Coward, so 'Cowardly' means by Coward
Lucifer and the rebel spirits cast out of heaven

explanation.surface: A timid remark about devilish characters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cowardly' looks like timid, but means 'of Noël Coward', the English playwright whose 1925 comedy has this title.
explanation.definitionFit: Coward's comedy shares its title with the rebel spirits thrown out of heaven with Satan.

clue.text: Would the author of such a novel be a man of letters?

definitions.text: Would the author of such a novel be a man of letters?

parts.words: Would the author of such a novel be a man of letters?
parts.note: a novel told through letters makes its writer literally a man of letters

explanation.surface: Asks whether a novelist of a certain kind earns the title of literary man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'man of letters' means a literary figure, but here it means someone writing in the form of correspondence.
explanation.definitionFit: Describes fiction told entirely through correspondence, such as Richardson's Pamela.

clue.text: Theatrical projection going some way to meet its audience

definitions.text: Theatrical projection going some way to meet its audience

parts.words: Theatrical projection going some way to meet its audience
parts.note: a part of the playing area that juts out beyond the proscenium into the auditorium

explanation.surface: Describes a part of a theatre that reaches out towards the spectators.
explanation.walkthrough: 'projection' could mean throwing the voice or a film, but here it is a physical structure sticking out.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the part of the stage extending in front of the curtain line towards the seats.

clue.text: Dreamscape of Alice and Joyce Carol?

definitions.text: Dreamscape of Alice and Joyce Carol?

parts.words: Dreamscape of Alice and Joyce Carol?
parts.note: Lewis Carroll's heroine dreams her adventures, and Joyce Carol Oates wrote a 1971 novel of the same title

explanation.surface: Asks what dream world two literary women share.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Joyce Carol' omits the surname Oates; her novel shares its title with the place Alice visits in Lewis Carroll's book.
explanation.definitionFit: Carroll's Alice dreams of a magical land, and Oates titled a novel after it.

clue.text: Sort of music provided for theatregoers?

definitions.meaning: instrumental music that tells a story or depicts a scene
the booklet handed to an audience listing cast and details

explanation.surface: A kind of music laid on for an audience at the theatre.
explanation.definitionFit: Descriptive music of that name tells a story, and the same word is the booklet sold at plays.

clue.text: William Rose Benet's traders from China

definitions.text: William Rose Benet's traders from China

parts.words: William Rose Benet's traders from China
parts.note: Benét's poem '... from Cathay', Cathay being an old name for China

explanation.surface: Names the Chinese traders in a poem by William Rose Benét.
explanation.walkthrough: William Rose Benét, an American poet, wrote 'Merchants from Cathay'; the clue gives the first word of the title.
explanation.definitionFit: Traders who buy and sell goods are the people named in Benét's poem title.

clue.text: Capital in novel has a romantic ring, being not far from Shangri La

definitions.text: Capital in novel has a romantic ring, being not far from Shangri La

indicators.note: in signals that the letters sit inside the words novel has a

explanation.surface: A city in a book sounds romantic, lying near the fabled paradise of Shangri-La.
explanation.walkthrough: The rest of the clue enlarges on the capital: Tibet's chief city sits in the Himalayan region where James Hilton set Shangri-La in Lost Horizon.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the capital of Tibet.

clue.text: 'Rising nineteen, I'll very soon be out there among the —s' (Colin MacInnes)

definitions.text: 'Rising nineteen, I'll very soon be out there among the —s' (Colin MacInnes)

parts.words: 'Rising nineteen, I'll very soon be out there among the —s' (Colin MacInnes)
parts.note: the teenage narrator of Absolute Beginners dreads joining the older generation

explanation.surface: A quotation from MacInnes's Absolute Beginners about growing up.
explanation.walkthrough: In Colin MacInnes's 1959 novel, the teenage narrator fears that soon he will no longer count as young.
explanation.definitionFit: An older person, past youth, is what the nearly nineteen-year-old fears becoming.

clue.text: His 1981 play was sure to be a hit

definitions.text: His 1981 play was sure to be a hit

parts.words: His 1981 play was sure to be a hit
parts.note: Jack ... 1981 play was called Smash!, another word for a hit

explanation.surface: Says a playwright's 1981 play was a guaranteed success.
explanation.walkthrough: Jack Rosenthal, the English dramatist, wrote the play Smash! (1981); a 'smash' is a hit, so its title made it 'sure to be a hit'.
explanation.definitionFit: The English dramatist Jack Rosenthal titled his 1981 play Smash!, slang for a hit.

clue.text: "I had as lief you would tell me of a mess of porridge", he said

definitions.text: "I had as lief you would tell me of a mess of porridge", he said

parts.words: "I had as lief you would tell me of a mess of porridge", he said
parts.note: a line spoken by the Welsh parson in Shakespeare's The Merry Wives of Windsor

explanation.surface: Identifies the speaker of a line about porridge.
explanation.walkthrough: The line comes from The Merry Wives of Windsor, spoken by the comic Welsh parson.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's Welsh parson in The Merry Wives of Windsor speaks the quoted line.

clue.text: "Her — is full of money" (The Great Gatsby)

definitions.text: "Her — is full of money" (The Great Gatsby)

parts.words: "Her — is full of money" (The Great Gatsby)
parts.note: Gatsby's famous remark about Daisy Buchanan's way of speaking

explanation.surface: A quotation from Fitzgerald about Daisy.
explanation.walkthrough: Gatsby says this of Daisy in F. Scott Fitzgerald's novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Gatsby hears wealth in the way Daisy speaks, the sound of her speech.

clue.text: Poet inclined to pontificate?

definitions.meaning: the head of the Catholic Church is the pontiff, whose role is to pontificate

explanation.surface: A poet with a tendency to lecture people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pontificate' usually means to sound off pompously, but literally it is what a pontiff, the head of the Roman Catholic Church, does.
explanation.definitionFit: Alexander Pope was an English poet, and the head of the Catholic Church is the pontiff.

clue.text: "It — this time of year", Gogarty thought

definitions.text: "It — this time of year", Gogarty thought

parts.words: "It — this time of year", Gogarty thought
parts.note: a line from Oliver St John Gogarty, the Irish poet and wit

explanation.surface: A quotation from the Irish writer Oliver St John Gogarty.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word is the negative contraction of 'is not' in Gogarty's line.

clue.text: Bulwer-Lytton's schoolmaster, a male animal

parts.note: a ram is a male sheep

explanation.surface: Bulwer-Lytton's teacher was a male beast.
explanation.walkthrough: Eugene Aram, the murderous schoolmaster, is the title figure of Edward Bulwer-Lytton's 1832 novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Eugene Aram is the schoolmaster-murderer in Bulwer-Lytton's novel.

clue.text: Weak leading men opposed to Carlyle's theme?

parts.note: anti means against or opposed to
Thomas Carlyle's lectures On Heroes, Hero-Worship, and the Heroic in History

explanation.surface: Feeble protagonists stand against Carlyle's great-man theory.
explanation.walkthrough: Thomas Carlyle, the Victorian essayist, lectured on great men in On Heroes (1841).
explanation.definitionFit: Central characters lacking traditional virtues such as courage are protagonists of the flawed kind.

clue.text: Violent ones follow violent delights, Friar Laurence warned

definitions.text: Violent ones follow violent delights, Friar Laurence warned

parts.words: Violent ones follow violent delights, Friar Laurence warned
parts.note: Friar Laurence in Romeo and Juliet says such delights have violent conclusions

explanation.surface: Friar Laurence's warning that pleasures can turn to violence.
explanation.walkthrough: Friar Laurence says in Romeo and Juliet: 'These violent delights have violent ends.'
explanation.definitionFit: The friar's line says violent pleasures bring violent conclusions.

clue.text: Modestine, perhaps, with some chaps, is on time that's the estimate

parts.note: Modestine is the donkey in Stevenson's Travels with a Donkey; she with some others makes several donkeys
S stands for is, as in the contraction it's
chaps are men

explanation.surface: Stevenson's donkey and some fellows are punctual, by one reckoning.
explanation.walkthrough: Modestine is the donkey Robert Louis Stevenson travelled with in the Cévennes; she plus some others are donkeys in the plural.
explanation.definitionFit: An appraisal is a valuation or judgement of worth or size.
